items.title: The Impact of Time Pressure on Perceptions of Difficulty in an Automation-Supported Task
items.abstract: As automation progressively becomes integrated into decision-making environments, understanding why users fail to engage automated systems optimally remains crucial. The present study examined whether perceptions of time pressure could impact subjective and objective difficulty and its influence on use of discretionary automation. Seventy participants completed a visual search task under untimed and timed conditions, sometimes with the option to engage an automated aid. Results indicated that the time pressure increased both subjective and objective difficulty. Furthermore, participants used automation more frequently under the timed conditions. Despite the availability of a highly accurate system, participants did not engage the automation at rates to fully overcome the effects of time pressure. These findings suggest that users may turn to automation for support when task demands begin to increase, but these engagement decisions may not be driven to maximize performance outcomes.

items.title: The Importance of Physiotherapy in a Conservative Treatment of Carpal Tunnel Syndrome
items.abstract: Purpose. The purpose of the study was to demonstrate the effect of selected physiotherapy methods in patients with a moderate form of carpal tunnel syndrome treated conservatively and to verify whether a one-month structured therapeutic programme leads to a measurable improvement in pain, joint mobility and swelling of the hand. Materials and Methods. An observational study was carried out in a group of 8 adult patients (4 women, 4 men) aged 39–71 years (mean age 56.25 years) with grade 2 carpal tunnel syndrome. Each patient underwent an entry examination comprising history taking, anthropometric measurement of upper-limb circumferences in the area of the forearm, wrist and metacarpal heads, goniometric measurement of the active and passive mobility of the carpometacarpal joint of the thumb in the sagittal and frontal planes using the SFTR method, and pain assessment on a numeric rating scale. The therapeutic programme lasted one month and consisted of 8 sessions of 50 minutes; it included kinesiotherapy, manual therapy, proprioceptive neuromuscular facilitation, stimulation of hand sensitivity, ultrasound applied to the palmar aspect of the carpometacarpal joint of the thumb (3 MHz, 50 Hz, pulse-pause ratio 1:2, intensity 1.0–1.6 W·cm⁻²) and kinesiology taping. Input and output values were compared using the one-tailed paired t-test at a level of significance α = 0.05. Results. The range of motion of the carpometacarpal joint of the thumb increased in both planes, for the active (sagittal plane p = 0.0001917; frontal plane p = 0.000005688) as well as for the passive range of motion (p = 0.00291 and p = 0.00002326). The intensity of pain decreased from a mean value of 4 to 2.625 (p = 0.00006782). The circumferences decreased in the area of the wrist (p = 0.01047) and of the metacarpal heads (p = 0.04749), while the forearm circumference remained unchanged. Conclusions. One month of targeted physiotherapy significantly reduced pain and swelling and improved the mobility of the thumb in patients with a moderate form of carpal tunnel syndrome. Conservative physiotherapeutic management combined with education in the principles of ergonomics can be recommended before considering surgical decompression in patients with a mild and moderate form of the syndrome.

items.title: The Influence of English Language Competence, Digital Literacy, Grit, and Technostress on Ship Crew Performance Mediated by Human Capital Capability
items.abstract: Crew performance determines the safety and operational efficiency of shipping companies, yet human factors remain the dominant cause of maritime accidents. This study aims to analyze the influence of English language competence, digital literacy, grit, and technostress on crew performance, with human capital capability serving as a mediating variable. A quantitative approach was employed, utilizing a survey of 316 seafarers from shipping companies in Indonesia, and the data were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) via SmartPLS. The results indicate that: 1) English language competence has a positive and significant effect on human capital capability; 2) Digital literacy has a positive and significant effect on human capital capability; 3) Grit has a positive and significant effect on human capital capability; 4) Technostress does not have a significant effect on human capital capability; 5) English language competence does not have a significant effect on crew performance; 6) Digital literacy does not have a significant effect on crew performance; 7) Grit has a positive and significant effect on crew performance; 8) Technostress does not have a significant effect on crew performance; 9) Human capital capability has a positive and significant effect on crew performance; 10) Human capital capability fully mediates the effect of English language competence on crew performance; 11) Human capital capability fully mediates the effect of digital literacy on crew performance; 12) Human capital capability partially mediates the effect of grit on crew performance; 13) Human capital capability does not mediate the effect of technostress on crew performance. Shipping companies need to enhance crew performance by strengthening human capital capability through maritime English training, digital literacy development, and mental resilience building. The novelty of this study lies in examining human capital capability as a mediating mechanism among Indonesian seafarers.

items.title: The Invisible Work Behind an Innovation: Discarded Alternatives, Limits of Validity, and the Memory of Decisions / El trabajo invisible detrás de una innovación: alternativas descartadas, límites de validez y memoria de las decisiones
items.abstract: ENGLISH This critical essay examines the knowledge that may be lost when technological innovation is described only through its visible outcome. Drawing on work on invisible labour, articulation work, design rationale, knowledge boundaries and organizational learning, it distinguishes the context-dependent rejection of an alternative from evidence of its general infeasibility. The paper proposes a six-field record for preserving actual alternatives considered, criteria, gaps in evidence, responsible decisions and conditions for reconsideration. A hypothetical photopolymer case illustrates the difference between a selected option, an option rejected under defined constraints and an option left unresolved by insufficient evidence. The proposed record has not been empirically validated, does not claim methodological priority, and is explicitly distinguished from the author's earlier technical publications. Version 1. English and Spanish editions deposited together. items.title: The Mandate as a Unit of Risk — paper outline
items.abstract: This research outline sets out the proposed argument, derivations, evidence requirements and limitations for “The Mandate as a Unit of Risk.” The proposed paper connects the authority under which an AI agent acts with the economics of task reliability, oversight and adverse outcomes. It treats the mandate as a versioned authority for a class of acts, enforced through a permission that can be refused before an act is executed. The research programme examines how a mandate can express an admissible set of model-and-oversight configurations and a quantitative risk appetite, with authority narrowing automatically on independently adjudicated evidence and widening only with an authorised human signature. It extends the task-value framework with the cost of refusal and escalation, examines calibration in financial services, and identifies the conditions and limitations of any proposed assurance statement. The outline distinguishes established precedents from candidate contributions and identifies simulation and empirical work still required. Publication status: This deposit is a research outline, not a completed or peer-reviewed paper. Proposed theoretical results, calibration procedures and empirical tests remain to be established. Cordier’s simulation layer has not been independently rerun; the outline states the assumptions on which its proposed analysis depends.

items.title: The Mediating Role of Job Insecurity in the Relationship Between Technology Threat Perception and Organizational Commitment: An Investigation on Artificial Intelligence Anxiety
items.abstract: This study examines the mediating role of job insecurity in the relationships between technology threat perception, artificial intelligence anxiety, and organizational commitment. Data were collected from 387 full-time employees across multiple sectors in Türkiye through a cross-sectional survey. The hypothesized model was tested using structural equation modeling (AMOS 24), following confirmatory factor analysis and bootstrap-based mediation analysis (5,000 resamples). Technology threat perception and AI anxiety were both positively associated with job insecurity, which in turn was negatively associated with organizational commitment. Both stressors also showed significant direct negative associations with organizational commitment, and bootstrap analysis confirmed significant indirect effects through job insecurity, indicating complementary partial mediation. To the best of the authors' knowledge, this is among the first studies to jointly model technology threat perception and AI anxiety as co-occurring antecedents of job insecurity within a single structural framework linking both to organizational commitment, extending cognitive stress appraisal theory, Conservation of Resources theory, and Social Exchange Theory to the context of AI-driven workplace change, with region-specific evidence from Türkiye.

items.title: The Mitral Valve Heart Team 2.0: Integrating Imaging, Surgery, Transcatheter Therapies and Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: The management of mitral valve disease is rapidly evolving, driven by advances in multimodality imaging, surgical techniques, transcatheter therapies, and artificial intelligence (AI). In this changing landscape, the traditional Heart Team model should evolve toward a more integrated and dynamic multidisciplinary approach. The “Mitral Valve Heart Team 2.0” may combine detailed anatomical and functional characterization with surgical expertise, transcatheter treatment options, and AI-assisted data integration to support individualized treatment strategies. Advanced imaging increasingly informs not only diagnosis but also procedural planning and patient selection, while AI may improve reproducibility of mitral regurgitation assessment, risk stratification, and phenotypic characterization. However, these technologies should augment rather than replace expert clinical judgment and shared decision-making. This Communication discusses the emerging components of this paradigm and proposes a practical framework in which imaging specialists, surgeons, interventional cardiologists, heart failure specialists, and data-driven tools interact throughout the patient pathway. The objective is not to create a larger Heart Team, but a more integrated one, capable of matching the right patient to the right treatment at the right time.

items.title: The Observer-Relative Interpretation Problem & The I or O Test™
items.abstract: The Observer-Relative Interpretation Problem & The I or O Test™ presents an evolving philosophical framework examining the relationship between observation, interpretation, identity, love, self-preservation, and continuity. The original working paper, developed October 23, 2026, investigates how different observers may encounter the same information yet arrive at different interpretations. It distinguishes physical and chemical information from meta-interpretation, proposing that the observer's perspective influences understanding without necessarily changing the underlying reality. An experimental appendix, developed October 28, 2026, introduces The I or O Test™, a proposed six-photograph observation exercise followed by personal explanation, a provisional trial period, and consideration of traceable behavioral evidence. The experiment introduces three observer-relative outcomes: I: Passed with insufficient evidence. O: Failed the experiment's stated criteria. i: The observed individual provided an explanation that convinced the observer. The appendix further develops the Birth Star Principle™, proposing that individuals differ in what they regard as essential to their self-preservation. Additional symbolic concepts include Pearly's Continuation, the collaboration of O and I through love, and the emergence of Newi. The central philosophical proposition is that observation does not confer complete knowledge of another individual. Interpretation remains provisional, and the observer must remain willing to correct their own understanding. This publication is an original, exploratory philosophical proposal. Its symbolic terminology and experimental classifications are not scientifically validated psychological assessments, diagnostic categories, or established physical laws. items.title: The Path of a Young Researcher: A Practical Guide for Students of the Presidential Academy
items.abstract: This practical guide, prepared by the Student Scientific Society of the Presidential Academy (RANEPA), supports students taking their first steps in research. It is structured as a journey map of eight stages: understanding science, finding sources, conducting research, writing, publishing, presenting, growing and getting support, and being part of the academic community. The guide explains how scientific knowledge differs from opinion, how academic degrees, titles and positions are organized, and how science is governed and funded in Russia. It covers systematic literature search, including eLIBRARY, CyberLeninka and the RANEPA library. It also covers research design (problem, object, subject, aim, objectives, hypothesis and methods) and the responsible use of artificial intelligence in line with the Academy’s Academic Integrity and AI Policy. Further sections address academic writing and the IMRAD structure, citation styles, plagiarism and originality, and choosing journals indexed in RSCI or listed by the Higher Attestation Commission and the Unified State List of Scientific Journals. They also explain how to recognize predatory publications, the peer-review process, and preparing conference presentations. Finally, the guide describes scholarships, grants, the student research portfolio and the structure of the Student Scientific Society. Each section includes step-by-step instructions, screenshots, QR codes to official resources and practical tips. A glossary of key terms is included. Keywords: young researcher, student research, academic writing, research design, scientific publishing, academic integrity, student scientific society, RANEPA

items.title: The Potential of AI-Powered Reflective Tools in Teacher Education
items.abstract: This chapter explores how generative artificial intelligence (AI) is influencing reflective practice in second language teacher education, along with the discussion on ethics and the developmental implications of AI-powered reflection. It conceptualizes AI-powered reflection as a form of technological mediation that alters how teaching experience is externalized and interpreted through algorithmic processes. Grounding in distributed cognition, this chapter positions AI as a cognitive artifact that shapes reflective activity while teacher professional meaning-making and accountability remains situated in teachers’ judgment. It shows how the influence of algorithmic mediation on reflective authority, agency and temporal depth has specific implications for professional novice teachers. Ethical considerations are presented as fundamental to the responsible integration of AI-powered reflective tools. The chapter further introduces a human-centered framework to inform their design and pedagogical use in teacher education and identifies future directions for research and practice that seek to sustain reflective depth and teacher agency within mentoring relationships and professional learning contexts. It concludes that AI can enhance reflective support when its use is guided by ethical commitments and remains aligned with the developmental purposes of professional development.

items.title: The Prestige: Benchmarking Cognitive Visual Reasoning using Magic Tricks
items.abstract: We introduce The Prestige, a video understanding benchmark that probes cognitive visual reasoning through professional magic performances, where deliberate misdirection challenges models to track events and explain unexpected outcomes. The benchmark comprises open-ended questions ranging from temporal and causal understanding to robustness against adversarial questions. Evaluation of leading open-source and proprietary VLMs reveals a substantial gap between even the strongest model and human performance. We also find systematic discrepancies between human and automated grading and identify recurring model failure modes. Ablations further show that models can select correct multiple-choice answers even when they fail to generate correct explanations independently, motivating further investigations into question formats. Together, these findings highlight limitations in both VLM reasoning and its evaluation, underscoring the need for more reliable video understanding models and more rigorous benchmarks.

items.title: The Relationship Between Breakfast Habits and Work Productivity Among Production Department Workers at PT Charoen Pokphand Indonesia in 2026
items.abstract: Work productivity reflects the extent to which workers are able to carry out their responsibilities effectively during the production process. Workers’ eating patterns, including whether they consume breakfast before starting their activities, may be relevant to their physical readiness and ability to perform their tasks. This study examined the association between breakfast habits and work productivity among production department workers at PT Charoen Pokphand Indonesia in 2026. A quantitative observational study using a cross-sectional design was carried out among 120 production department workers, from whom 55 respondents were included as the study sample. Information regarding breakfast habits and work productivity was obtained through questionnaires. The collected data were subsequently analyzed using the Chi-Square test with Continuity Correction. Among the 55 respondents, 40 workers (72.7%) reported that they did not have a regular breakfast habit, whereas 15 workers (27.3%) reported having a breakfast habit. Regarding productivity, 37 respondents (67.3%) were categorized as having low work productivity, while 18 respondents (32.7%) were categorized as having high productivity. Statistical analysis produced a p-value of 0.003 (p < 0.05), demonstrating a significant association between breakfast habits and work productivity. The proportion of workers with high productivity was greater among those who reported having breakfast than among those who did not. The study concludes that breakfast habits are significantly associated with work productivity among production department workers at PT Charoen Pokphand Indonesia. These findings support the consideration of healthy breakfast practices as part of occupational health promotion and efforts to encourage adequate nutritional intake among workers

items.title: The relationship of autonomy with hybrid worker well-being and productivity - the mediating role of managerial culture
items.abstract: Purpose Knowledge work is extensively location-independent, making flexible work designs more common. However, organizations foster various practices regarding the level of autonomy and control, affecting employee well-being and productivity. To support strategic and operative work design, this paper aims to explain the relationship of autonomy with hybrid worker well-being and productivity, considering the mediating role of managerial culture. Design/methodology/approach This paper describes a quantitative survey featuring 1,057 respondents. It tests with a regression analysis a hypothesized model, in which the level of individual work autonomy, mediated by managerial culture, predicts well-being and productivity. Findings The analysis indicated that decision-making autonomy has a direct positive relationship with productivity. Furthermore, autonomy in working practices has a direct positive relationship with both well-being and productivity. Managerial culture mediates the relationship between decision-making autonomy and both outcome variables. Originality/value This paper provides empirical evidence of the relationship of autonomy with hybrid worker well-being and productivity. The academic value of this paper lies in the multiple dimensions of autonomy it addresses, yielding novel data on the outcomes in a comparative manner. As a pragmatic contribution, it provides input to managerial culture design.

items.title: The Relationships Between Artificial Intelligence-Induced Job Insecurity, Affective Commitment, Job Performance and Turnover Intention
items.abstract: This study examines the relationships between artificial intelligence-induced job insecurity, affective commitment, job performance, and turnover intention, with particular attention to the mediating roles of affective commitment and job performance. The analyses were conducted using structural equation modeling to assess the direct and indirect relationships among the variables. Data were collected from 400 employees working in different sectors through online and face-to-face surveys using a convenience sampling method. The findings indicate that AI-induced job insecurity is positively associated with turnover intention and negatively associated with affective commitment, whereas its direct association with job performance is not statistically significant. Affective commitment is positively associated with job performance and negatively associated with turnover intention. The mediation analyses indicate that affective commitment significantly mediates the relationships between AI-induced job insecurity and turnover intention and between AI-induced job insecurity and job performance. In contrast, the mediating role of job performance in the relationship between AI-induced job insecurity and turnover intention is not supported. Overall, the findings suggest that affective commitment represents an important explanatory pathway in the relationships between AI-induced job insecurity and employees’ work-related outcomes.

items.title: The Role of AI in Dementia Caregiving - A Scoping Review.
items.abstract: Background: Dementia is a growing public health issue, one that burdens many, with a heavy reliance on familial relationships for support and care. This is an especially pressing issue within ethnically diverse (ED) communities. In parallel, Artificial Intelligence (AI) is also a rapidly growing industry, with many of its aspects being used in healthcare and patient management. Healthcare and AI have a reciprocal relationship. Today, AI can assist with many aspects of healthcare, such as assisting dementia caregivers through providing additional support. While this is a strong approach, before widespread use, it is important to be aware of its benefits, harms and ethical implications, since there is limited knowledge available on the topic and uninformed use can be detrimental. Aims and objectives: The aim of this study is to understand how AI can be used within the role of dementia caregiving. The objective is to understand AI uses’ barriers, enablers and the ethical issues that are prevalent, specifically for ED communities, dissecting if AI use for such sensitive topics would be appropriate or even feasible. Methods: For this scoping review various databases would be searched for articles on AI use in dementia caregiving and then screened in Covidence for relevance before data analysis. Grey literature would also be screened and reviewed. Significance: Dementia is a public health priority, it burdens many, especially within ED communities making it important to identify tools to assist with caregiving. This study would give an insight into how AI could be appropriately involved in dementia caregiving without imposing ethically.

items.title: The Role of Artificial Intelligence in Mediating the Influence of Language Literacy on the Academic Writing Skills of Politeknik Negeri Ambon Students
items.abstract: This study aims to analyze the influence of Language Literacy on Academic Writing Ability with Artificial Intelligence as a mediating variable in Ambon State Polytechnic students. Academic writing ability is one of the important competencies that students must have in producing quality scientific work. However, the development of Artificial Intelligence technology has changed the learning patterns and academic writing processes of students. This study uses a quantitative approach with a survey method. The study population was Ambon State Polytechnic students, with a sample of 50 respondents determined using a purposive sampling technique. Data were collected through questionnaires and analyzed using Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) based on Partial Least Square (PLS) with the help of SmartPLS 4. The results of the study indicate that Language Literacy has a positive and significant effect on Artificial Intelligence, Artificial Intelligence has a positive and significant effect on Academic Writing Ability, while Language Literacy has a positive but insignificant effect on Academic Writing Ability. In addition, Artificial Intelligence is proven to significantly mediate the relationship between Language Literacy and Academic Writing Ability. The results of the study indicate that Artificial Intelligence acts as a full mediator in this relationship. This finding indicates that the improvement of students' academic writing ability is not only determined by language literacy skills, but also by the ability to utilize Artificial Intelligence effectively in the learning process and academic writing.

items.title: The Role of Artificial Intelligence in the Development of Creativity Skills According to Teachers and Students
items.abstract: The increasing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into education has renewed debates on the nature of creativity. This study examines the role of artificial intelligence in the development of creativity skills among middle school teachers and students through comparative perspectives. Using a qualitative case study design, the research involved 87 participants—42 teachers from different subject areas and 45 eighth-grade students—from public middle schools in Bursa, Turkey, during the 2025–2026 academic year. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews and analyzed via content analysis. The findings reveal that AI plays a dual role in the creative process: it facilitates idea generation and imagination, yet may restrict originality when used without pedagogical guidance. While students tend to view artificial intelligence as a tool that accelerates production, teachers emphasize risks such as cognitive offloading and superficial learning. Artificial intelligence becomes an effective educational tool only when embedded within ethically grounded, teacher-guided, and AI literacy–oriented frameworks. Subject-based analyses show that, particularly in Science and Mathematics, teachers position AI as a supportive cognitive partner that facilitates visualization and conceptual understanding, yet caution that unguided use may replace deep learning with surface-level content production.

items.title: The Smart School Model: Integrating Intelligent Agents and IoT for Autonomous, Ethical and Reproducible Educational Management
items.abstract: Smart-school projects increasingly combine sensors, dashboards and artificial intelligence, but their managerial value remains weak when attendance, access control, energy use and reporting operate as isolated modules. This paper proposes a Smart School Management System (SSMS) in which Internet-of-Things observations are transformed into auditable decisions through a policy-constrained multi-agent architecture. Unlike component-level smart-campus prototypes, the contribution is an orchestration model linking perception agents, decision agents and a coordination agent under privacy, traceability and human-oversight constraints. The empirical part uses the open UCI Occupancy Detection dataset (20,560 labelled records) to validate the perception layer on a reproducible occupancy-classification task. Trained on 8,143 records and tested on 12,417 records, logistic regression achieved 98.34% accuracy and 0.9659 F1-score, outperforming a simple light-threshold rule (94.36% accuracy, 0.8961 F1). These results validate only the occupancy-perception component under the stated open-data protocol; they do not validate the complete smart-school system or institutional deployment. The paper therefore advances a reproducible, ethically governed and practically deployable direction for autonomous educational management.

items.title: The Study of Digital Transformation, Artificial Intelligence and Their Implications for Future Research
items.abstract: Digital transformation changes the conditions under which organizations produce and use knowledge. Artificial intelligence adds new ways to search, predict, generate, and evaluate information. Yet greater use of these tools does not establish that research becomes more reliable or more original. This paper develops a critical narrative review and descriptive secondary-data analysis to examine that distinction. Selected publications on organizational change, AI-assisted work, scientific discovery, and governance provide the conceptual foundation. Published statistics from Stanford's AI Index and Eurostat illustrate changes in adoption between 2023 and 2025. The two series are analysed separately because their populations and measurement procedures differ. The evidence indicates expanding use, but adoption statistics cannot demonstrate causal improvements in research quality. An original conceptual framework links digital foundations and AI capabilities with changes in research practice, conditioned by human expertise, institutional arrangements, and governance. Four propositions translate the framework into questions for future testing. The proposed agenda prioritizes reproducibility, task-specific evaluation, skill development, equitable participation, and preservation of intellectual diversity. The paper concludes that future research should evaluate the complete knowledge-production process, including verification and correction costs, rather than treating faster output as sufficient evidence of progress. No primary survey, experiment, or model validation is claimed. The contribution is an integrated account of how organizations can study AI-enabled transformation while maintaining the evidentiary standards needed for credible knowledge

items.title: The Usability of Ranked Choice Voting in Digital Ballot Formats
items.abstract: ObjectiveThree digital ranked choice voting ballots were investigated to assess the impact of formatting on usability.BackgroundRanked choice voting (RCV) is a ballot format that allows voters to rank candidate choices in order of preference. The design of the ballot has a notable impact on usability, and this remains a challenge for RCV.MethodThis experiment investigated the usability of three RCV electronic ballot formats (bubble grid, column, and hand-numbered). Completion times, errors, subjective usability ratings, and trust data were collected.ResultsThe three formats took subjects 50-70 seconds on average to vote for a single contest. The ballots also had high error rates, which ranged from 23-38%. The hand-numbered format had the worst performance, as it had the highest completion times, error rates, and the lowest subjective usability ratings.ConclusionThis research highlights usability issues with RCV digital ballots. The formats tested were inefficient and ineffective, and performed poorly in comparison to previously tested plurality digital ballots.ApplicationThis experiment raises concerns about the scalability of RCV to larger elections. Ballots with RCV take longer to vote on and have higher error rates, which should be taken into consideration by election administrators.

items.title: The Use of Generative AI in Second Language Writing: Opportunities, Challenges, and Future Directions
items.abstract: The development of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping second language (L2) writing by introducing new forms of interaction between learners and intelligent technologies. This conceptual paper examines the potential opportunities and critical challenges of GenAI in L2 writing, drawing on a purposively selected body of recent scholarship. It suggests that GenAI can provide contingent support throughout the writing process, facilitate idea generation and revision, and expand opportunities for multilingual composing through L1-mediated and translanguaging practices. At the same time, excessive reliance on AI may lead to cognitive offloading and weaken learners’ engagement in higher-order writing processes. Concerns about inaccurate information and fabricated citations further highlight the need for independent verification and critical AI literacy. Moreover, unequal access to technological resources, AI literacy, and educational support may contribute to an emerging AI divide and reproduce existing educational and linguistic inequalities. The paper argues that the pedagogical value of GenAI depends on how it is integrated into learners’ writing processes and on whether it supports sustained engagement, learner agency, and reflective thinking and decision-making without displacing their intellectual and authorial responsibilities.

items.title: Topological Multi-Connectivity of Distributed Cognitive Systems: Pairwise-Contact “Foams”, Individuality Without Dissolution, and a Falsiable Research Program
items.abstract: Can an agent be in contact with all other agents without being dissolved in them? We give this question a precise topological form. A pairwise-contact foam is a family of regions ("bubbles") of a state space with pairwise disjoint interiors, which represent the preserved individuality of each agent, such that every two regions touch, which represents connection, ideally along a set of positive size. We show that the naive formulation of the condition is degenerate unless the regions are regular closed with nonempty interior, and that point contact is cheap in dimension \( \ge2 \) while contact along arcs is impossible in the plane for more than four disks. We then prove that foams exist for every number \( N\ge2 \) of regions and, in the infinite-dimensional Hilbert space \( \ell^2 \), for countably infinitely many regions covering the whole space: the regions \( D_k=\{x:|x_k|\ge|x_j|\ \forall j\} \) meet pairwise along codimension-one walls \( x_k=\pm x_l \). In dimension three and on orientable surfaces of higher genus the planar obstruction is bypassed as well. Gluing along contact sets leaves every piece intact, which is the formal sense of "union without dissolution". Pairwise contact is strictly weaker than the Wada property, and riddled basins are a degenerate, non-proper case. For empirical use we separate three quantities that are easily confused: the global separation \( d(C_i,C_j) \) of two regions, the switching distance \( d(x,C_j) \) from a given state, and the activation distance to the contact set, together with intervention-specific versions that depend on an actuation model. We replace a single adjacency density by the spectrum of separations, a threshold-free completion scale, and a persistent nerve, with explicit limits on what the nerve proves, dimension-aware null models, and a rule that unsupported regions make a test inconclusive rather than being deleted. We define preservation of an agent's own control pattern so that it includes distinguishability of agents, give a confirmatory test of the composite hypothesis H4 whose unit of analysis is the independent replicate, and outline falsifiable programs in morphospace navigation by bioelectric interventions and in the information topology of human, AI, and biological collectives, including prediction of group fragmentation. No empirical result is claimed. The interpretive layer (cognitive light cone, "noosphere") is kept strictly apart from the mathematical and testable layers.

items.title: Towards a Cognitive Behavioural Occupational Health Practice
items.abstract: This chapter outlines the personal and professional foundations of the cognitive behavioural approach developed for occupational health practice. Both occupational health and cognitive behavioural therapy became a vocation for me, providing a stabilising and meaningful thread that supported my movement beyond personal adversity and shaped my progression from nursing into trauma therapy and expert-witness work. The chapter traces a 40-year professional journey alongside the evolution of occupational health, from its earlier focus on industrial injury to its current role as a clinically grounded specialty. It considers how changes in the nature of work, together with increasing recognition of psychological and social influences on health, have reshaped contemporary occupational health practice. My thinking has been strongly influenced by the work of Gordon Waddell, Tom Cox, Cary Cooper and others whose research laid the foundations for biopsychosocial and psychologically informed approaches to work and health. These influences supported my development as both an occupational health practitioner and cognitive behavioural therapist and continue to guide my clinical reasoning. This chapter therefore introduces the values, evidence base and reasoning that underpin the cognitive behavioural approach explored throughout this book.

items.title: Towards Task-Oriented Semantic Communication: A Survey on Technologies, Opportunities, and Challenges
items.abstract: The growing demand for intelligent and adaptive services is accelerating the transition from conventional communication systems to semantic communication. Task-Oriented Semantic Communication (ToSC) has emerged as an efficient framework that reduces communication cost by transmitting only task-relevant information for downstream processing. This survey reviews the theoretical foundations, system architectures, and enabling technologies of ToSC, providing a taxonomy of design strategies spanning collaborative edge inference, end-to-end optimization, and multi-agent cooperation. Key technologies, including deep learning-based semantic representation and adaptive joint source-channel coding, are discussed. Device heterogeneity and partial observability are examined alongside recent tasks' performance evaluations, such as classification and recognition. The survey also discusses the integration of large-scale multimodal foundation models into semantic encoders for zero-shot task adaptation, continual learning frameworks for on-device semantic processing, cooperative multi-agent reasoning with interpretable information exchange, and cross-layer co-design within AI-native 6G infrastructures, leveraging reconfigurable intelligent surfaces and digital twins. By consolidating existing knowledge and identifying key design trade-offs in latency, accuracy, and bandwidth efficiency, this work aims to serve as both a reference and a roadmap for advancing ToSC toward reliable and resource-efficient communication in 6G and beyond.

items.title: Tracekit Box: Running AI Agents in Micro-VMs Where Every Way Out Is Decided and Signed
items.abstract: AI agents now install packages, call model APIs with their operators' keys and change code in repositories that deploy to production. The network, credentials and write access they need are also how they can leak data, steal a key or change a system nobody approved. Sandboxes contain an agent but leave little evidence of what crossed their boundary; tracing records what happened but contains nothing. We present Tracekit Box, an open-source system (MIT, v0) that does both. Each job runs in its own Firecracker micro-VM with no network card. The only ways out are doors on the host, served over vsock: commands, outbound connections, secrets, model calls and the workspace patch. At every door a Tracekit signer the agent cannot reach decides what passes and signs it into one run per box. Names are resolved on the host; private and cloud-metadata addresses are always refused; secrets never enter the VM, which sees placeholders the host proxy swaps for real values only in one header for bound hosts; and changes come back as a patch applied file by file after the signer decides each file. Box fails closed, and each job ends as a .tkb bundle anyone can verify offline. All 13 end-to-end checks pass on a real KVM runner (the test that runs them takes 28.5 s, including image pull and boot); 15 fuzz targets on the trust boundary produced nine findings, all fixed; and the demo run's 102 signed records verify. Box does not yet run Firecracker's jailer, needs a co-located signer, and records processes inside the VM only where they cross a door.

items.abstract: A dated test protocol, not a pre-registration, for a study of Estonia's policy on identifiers for artificial intelligence (AI) agents. It uses explaining-outcome process tracing on its theory-first path. The protocol sets out the rival explanations, the observables that bear on them and how each is tested, the coding design with a human second coder, the collection rules, and the author's interventions in the process, each with its date. items.title: Tracing the Influence of Retrieved Literature on Scientific Ideation in LLMs
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate research ideas from scientific literature. Existing systems combine literature retrieval with search, generation, and refinement, making it difficult to determine how the retrieval strategy itself shapes the ideas generated. We isolate this contribution by comparing five retrieval strategies and a No Literature baseline under a shared generation protocol, using 45,000 ideas across 15 machine learning topics and ten open-weight models. Relative to no literature basline, all five retrieval strategies reduce diversity among ideas generated from the same set of papers by $5.6\%$--$17.9\%$, while most increase diversity by $10.2\%$--$18.1\%$ when ideas from different sets are pooled. Effects on idea quality and novelty are modest on average but vary across topics. We further apply a JSD-based attribution method to trace the influence of individual input papers on each idea's motivation, core idea, approach, and validation. In $79.3\%$ of ideas, only one or two distinct papers receive the highest attribution scores across these four parts. These leading sources often recur across ideas generated from the same set of papers, and groups with more varied source attribution contain more diverse ideas ($r=0.70$). These findings motivate various sets of literature and the use of attribution to guide the choice of sources for subsequent ideas.

items.title: Trained on Civilians, Deployed on Soldiers: Behavioral Validity and the Governance of Military Mental Health Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is moving from pilot programs into the routine delivery of military mental health care. Predictive models already scan Veterans Health Administration records to flag veterans at high risk of suicide; models trained on Army Study to Assess Risk and Resilience in Servicemembers data can now stratify suicide risk up to a decade after soldiers leave active service, and generative AI models are being positioned to deliver triage, peer support, and low-intensity psychological interventions. The frameworks that govern responsible military AI have not kept up. The Department of Defense Responsible Artificial Intelligence Strategy and Implementation Pathway, NATO’s principles of responsible use, and allied instruments such as the United Kingdom’s JSP 936 provide lifecycle assurance for AI-enabled capability, but none of them makes specific provision for the therapeutic encounter. That omission exposes service members to what this commentary terms a recognition-action gap. Systems trained predominantly on civilian data can transcribe the words of military distress accurately while misreading their clinical meaning: moral injury classified as fear-based trauma, minimized suicidality scored as low risk, routine operational vernacular flagged as threat. The risk is compounded because the boundary between clinical care and occupational capability is porous in the armed forces. The military command exception to the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act Privacy Rule and command notification under Department of Defense Instruction 6490.08 mean that outputs generated for care could lawfully reach deployability, security clearance, and administrative decisions, with predictable consequences for help-seeking. This commentary proposes behavioral validity, the demonstrated capability to safely manage the behavioral presentations of the population a system will actually serve, as a core governance requirement for mental health AI in defense settings. It specifies 4 conditions of use: clinically supervised pre-fielding assessment, therapeutic firewalling, moral injury and cultural competency, and meaningful human control. Defense health systems should not wait for civilian regulators to notice the gap. They are well placed to define the standard.

items.title: TrussTutor-Bench: Benchmarking large language models on solution accuracy, sycophancy, and error detection in statics
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have rapidly become a default source of help for students in science and engineering courses. In foundational engineering mechanics courses such as statics, students routinely use these tools to check answers, work through partial solutions, and ask for explanations. Effective tutoring in this setting requires more than a correct final answer. A model must also confirm correct work when a student doubts it, and identify errors in flawed work. Existing benchmarks evaluate LLMs primarily on final-answer accuracy, so it is unclear whether models that can solve mechanics problems also have the other technical capabilities that tutoring depends on. Here we introduce TrussTutor-Bench, a benchmark of 200 verified two-dimensional truss problems paired with automatically generated student solutions, and use it to evaluate thirteen LLMs on solution accuracy, sycophancy, and error detection. Baseline accuracy ranged from 64.5% to 97.0%. Every model detected nearly all injected errors in synthetic flawed student work (90.4% to 100%), so error detection did not distinguish models under these clean conditions. Sycophancy did. When a student insisted that correct work was wrong, models rejected correct solutions to problems they had themselves solved in 1.6% to 50.0% of cases. These results show that performance varies widely across models: the leading models solve, check, and defend student work nearly perfectly, while others are far less reliable, particularly when a student doubts correct work. TrussTutor-Bench provides a verified, extensible standard for determining which models are technically reliable enough to put in front of students. Follow-up work must now focus on teaching rather than technical capability, drawing on learning science to determine whether LLM help leads students to understand the material or simply to reach the right answer.

items.title: Trust or Scrutiny? The Technology Readiness Paradox in Travel Planning With Generative Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence now drafts travel itineraries that travelers cannot easily verify. Integrating privacy calculus theory with a dual-pathway trust model, this study examines how system attributes shape tourist trust and continued usage, and how technology readiness conditions those links. A two-wave panel (433 Chinese and European travelers), a validation wave (372), and 42 interviews were analyzed using structural equation modeling, importance–performance map analysis, fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis, and thematic analysis. Data transparency and content authenticity raised both cognitive and affective trust, and affective trust sustained continued usage most strongly. Technology readiness reversed the expected pattern: readier travelers scrutinized fluent output rather than relying on it, weakening the behavioral effect of trust. Providers should replace generic privacy notices with in-context, verifiable data-use disclosures and checkable citations, and segment interfaces so that ready travelers receive verification tools and less-ready travelers receive reassurance. Regulators can make verifiability, not fluency, the disclosure standard.

items.title: Trusted but Not Fully Verified: Generative AI Use and Exposure to Errors in Clinical Documentation Among Healthcare Professionals
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools are entering clinical documentation ahead of institutional governance, and little is known about whether clinicians who rely on them also check their output, particularly in Central and Eastern Europe. This study characterized regular GenAI use for documentation, verification practices, and exposure to clinically relevant errors among healthcare professionals at a Romanian tertiary center, and identified the attitudes independently associated with regular use. Methods: In a cross-sectional survey of 126 physicians, residents, nurses, and public health specialists (46.0% of 315 invited), regular use was defined as at least weekly use for documentation during the preceding three months. Composites measured AI literacy, trust in output accuracy, perceived confidentiality risk, perceived usefulness, documentation burden, and intention; emotional exhaustion was measured with the Maslach Burnout Inventory. Correlates of regular use were examined with bootstrap-validated multivariable logistic regression, and differences in burden and exhaustion with propensity-score overlap weighting. Results: Regular use was reported by 56 participants (44.4%; 95% confidence interval [CI] 36.1–53.2), mostly with ChatGPT (89.3%) for referral and discharge letters (78.6%) and discharge summaries (69.6%). Users verified a mean of 70.3% (95% CI 65.6–75.0) of outputs line by line, and 36 (64.3%; 95% CI 51.2–75.5) had encountered at least one clinically relevant error. Among users, higher trust was associated with a lower proportion of outputs verified (Spearman ρ = −0.31; p = 0.020). Concern about factual errors was common in both groups (73.2% vs. 77.1%), whereas confidentiality concern, perceived insufficient training, and fear of liability were less frequent among users. Higher trust (adjusted odds ratio [OR] 2.36 per 10 points; 95% CI 1.34–4.15), higher perceived usefulness (OR 1.90; 1.03–3.50), and lower perceived risk (OR 0.49; 0.29–0.83) were independently associated with regular use (optimism-corrected area under the curve 0.905). After overlap weighting, differences in documentation burden (−4.8 points; 95% CI −12.1 to 2.6) and emotional exhaustion (−1.7; −5.9 to 2.5) were not statistically significant but were imprecisely estimated. Conclusions: Regular GenAI use coexisted with incomplete verification and frequent error exposure and was linked to trust and perceived usefulness; AI literacy and training were not independently associated with use once these attitudes were accounted for. Associations with documentation burden and emotional exhaustion were inconclusive. Institutions should treat verification as a distinct, trainable behavior and pair access with explicit confidentiality guidance.

items.title: Two Birds with One Stone: Skill-Augmented Generation via Unified Retrieval and Utilization
items.abstract: Skills, as reusable external knowledge, have demonstrated substantial potential to enhance the ability of Large Language Models (LLMs) to solve complex tasks. However, existing skill-augmented generation methods typically rely on separate models for skill retrieval and skill utilization, resulting in disconnected optimization of these two processes. To address this gap, we propose Skill-Uni, a unified reinforcement learning framework that jointly optimizes skill retrieval and utilization. Specifically, we adopt a generative skill retrieval paradigm that enables a single model to both learn how to retrieve relevant skills and leverage them for task solving. To effectively train this unified framework, we introduce a two-stage training strategy consisting of warm-up instruction tuning and GRPO, allowing the model to progressively improve its skill retrieval and utilization capabilities. Extensive experiments on five skill-related benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of Skill-Uni, yielding average performance gains of 66.59% and 34.82% over the base Qwen3-4B and LLaMA3.1-8B models, respectively. Besides, Skill-Uni is compatible with various skill retrieval engines, demonstrating its flexibility and generalizability. Additional in-depth analyses also provide insights into the effectiveness of Skill-Uni.

items.title: Two-Stage Clipping: Linear-Time Approximate and Exact Mixed-Norm Projections for Transformers
items.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) based on Transformer architectures have achieved remarkable performance across artificial intelligence tasks, but their computational cost remains a major bottleneck. Structured sparsification provides a promising approach to reducing this cost. In particular, $\ell_{1,\infty}$ projections can induce column-wise sparsity in model matrices, but existing proximal methods (Prox) typically require $\mathcal{O}(nm\log(nm))$ operations for matrices in $\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}$, limiting their computational and energy efficiency. In this paper, we introduce Two-Stage Clipping (TSC), an efficient structured sparsification operator inspired by bilevel optimization. Rather than solving a bilevel optimization problem in the strict sense, TSC decomposes the computation into two successive stages. First, group-level quantities are projected to allocate the global sparsity budget and identify active groups. Second, the resulting values are used as group-wise clipping thresholds for the matrix coefficients. For square attention matrices ($n \times n$), the complexity of our TSC method is $O(n^2)$, which is linear in the number of matrix coefficients. We establish a theoretical bound on the discrepancy between TSC and the exact proximal projection and show on synthetic data that the additional Euclidean approximation cost remains small in practice. Extensive benchmarks demonstrate substantial runtime improvements over proximal baselines and validate the theoretical norm identities underlying the proposed construction.

items.title: Type of manuscript: Review Article
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming an important technology in health care and is increasingly being explored in hospital pharmacy practice. Hospital pharmacists manage large amounts of medication-related information, including prescriptions, patient medical records, laboratory values, drug interactions, adverse drug reactions, medication histories and inventory data. AI-based technologies can analyse these data rapidly and may assist pharmacists in identifying medication-related problems, improving workflow and supporting clinical decision-making. Recent literature describes applications of AI in prescription screening, medication-error detection, adverse drug event detection, pharmacovigilance, medication reconciliation, dose optimization, clinical decision support, antimicrobial stewardship, inventory management and medication adherence Machine learning, deep learning and natural language processing are among the major technologies used in pharmacy-related AI applications. These technologies can identify patterns in electronic health records and clinical documentation that may be difficult to recognize manually. However, AI should be considered a support tool rather than a complete replacement for pharmacists. Concerns related to data quality, privacy algorithmic bias, explainability, cybersquatting, cost training and clinical validation remain important. Successful implementation therefore requires collaboration between pharmacists, physicians, information technology professionals, hospital administrators and AI developers. The review discusses the major applications, advantages, limitations, ethical considerations and future perspectives of AI in hospital pharmacy practice.

items.title: Understanding Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Audit in Nigeria: Will AI Replace the Auditor? A Qualitative Phenomenological Inquiry
items.abstract: This study qualitatively inquired into artificial intelligence and the future of audit in Nigeria, specifically investigating whether AI will replace the human auditor. A qualitative phenomenological design was adopted. Twenty-eight (28) participants were purposively selected across Lagos, Abuja, and Port Harcourt, comprising Big 4 and mid-tier audit partners, audit managers/seniors with 10+ years of experience, ICAN/ANAN/FRCN regulators, and audited clients including CFOs and Audit Committee chairs. Data were collected via semi-structured indepth interviews between January and May 2025. Data saturation was achieved at the 23rd interview. Thematic analysis was performed using the Braun and Clarke (2006) framework assisted by NVivo. Results reveal that AI is augmenting, not replacing, human auditors. Four distinct AI implementation levels emerged: Assisted Audit (e.g., IDEA, Excel), Augmented Audit (e.g., Power BI, ACL), Autonomous Testing (e.g., RPA, Machine Learning anomaly detection), and Advisory Assurance (e.g., Generative AI for reporting). AI deployment improved audit efficiency by 60% and increased anomaly detection from 35% to 82%. Key barriers to adoption include technophobia (78%), unstructured client data (72%), tool costs (65%), and a regulatory vacuum regarding AI audit evidence under ISA 500 (60%). The study proposes a Human-AI Collaboration Model (70-30 Model), where AI performs 70% of routine data tasks, and human auditors provide 30% high-level professional judgement, ethics, and skepticism. This represents the first phenomenological study in Nigeria exploring the lived experiences of senior practitioners on the AI replacement debate.

items.title: University students’ overreliance on generative AI feedback in the learning process: the effects of perceived cognitive load, cognitive offloading, and metacognitive monitoring
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) has introduced an important question in education, when AI provides immediate and reliable feedback, do students use it as a learning support tool or gradually rely on it as a substitute for their own cognitive efforts? Drawing on Cognitive Load Theory, Cognitive Offloading Theory, and Metacognitive Monitoring Theory, this study develops a theoretical model to explain the formation process of undergraduate students’ overreliance on GAI feedback. Specifically, this study examines the relationships among perceived cognitive load, cognitive offloading, and overreliance on GAI feedback, while further exploring how metacognitive monitoring levels shape this process. A questionnaire survey was conducted among 600 undergraduate students, and structural equation modeling was performed using AMOS 31.0. The results showed that perceived cognitive load significantly and positively predicted cognitive offloading, which further contributed to students’ overreliance on GAI feedback. Meanwhile, perceived cognitive load also directly predicted overreliance on GAI feedback. Bootstrap analysis further confirmed that cognitive offloading mediated the relationship between perceived cognitive load and overreliance on GAI feedback. In addition, this study established separate structural equation models for students with different levels of metacognitive monitoring and found distinct patterns in the formation of GAI feedback overreliance. Specifically, students with lower metacognitive monitoring were more likely to be influenced by cognitive pressure during learning, showing a more prominent direct relationship between perceived cognitive load and GAI feedback overreliance. This finding suggests that these students tend to rely more directly on GAI feedback when facing higher cognitive demands. In contrast, students with higher metacognitive monitoring demonstrated a more evident cognitive regulation process, in which cognitive offloading played a more important role in linking perceived cognitive load with GAI feedback overreliance. This indicates that these students may actively adjust their cognitive resource allocation when using GAI, although continuous cognitive offloading may still increase their dependence on AI-generated feedback.

items.title: Unpacking Ethical, Privacy, And Governance Risks in AI-IoT Based Healthcare Environments: A thematic analysis
items.abstract: Objective: The paper aimed to examine ethical, privacy, and governance challenges in AI-IoT (Artificial Intelligence-based Internet of Things) healthcare environments. Design: A total of 39 peer-reviewed open-access studies were screened and used for a systematic review using the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) framework. A multi-stage thematic analysis was used for identifying recurring patterns within the literature and answering the research questions. Results/outcomes: The identified challenges in the AI-IoT healthcare ecosystems, arising from the thematic analysis, are privacy and continuous surveillance, algorithmic bias and lack of explainability, limitations for informed consent, and fragmented governance and accountability. Conclusion: The findings, in sync with STS theory, indicate that challenges in AI-IoT healthcare systems cannot be addressed solely through technological innovations. In response, the study proposed an Integrated Human-Centric Trust Framework to integrate human intervention with technological advancements.

items.title: Unraveling Structure and Spectroscopic Signatures of Pt/γ-Al2O3 via an Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Simulation Framework
items.abstract: Supported subnanometer clusters have attracted significant attention in catalysis. Yet, it is challenging to resolve their structural evolution, particularly in the presence of adsorbates. Here, we present an artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled simulation framework that integrates machine learning force field (MLFF) construction, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, and ML-assisted infrared (IR) and X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) spectra analysis to investigate the restructuring of supported subnanometer clusters. Using Pt10/γ-Al2O3(110) as a model system, we explored the CO-induced restructuring of the cluster under different conditions. The simultaneous machine learning (ML)-spectra elucidate a strong interplay among adsorbate coverage, cluster restructuring, and cluster-support interaction. This work sheds light on the complex dynamics of supported subnanometer clusters that is extendible to other systems.

items.title: Unsupervised AI-platform for Virus-Agnostic Therapeutic Targets Discovery from Multi-Omics Datasets
items.abstract: Here, we developed ViralTensors, an unsupervised artificial intelligence (AI) platform that employs Nonnegative Matrix Factorization (NMF) and Weighted NMF (WNMF) for integration of multidimensional datasets and extraction of interpretable latent features. We demonstrate that ViralTensors extracts biologically relevant host regulatory programs and previously unrecognized associations within complex virus–host interactions from global transcriptomic datasets with virus–host protein interaction data. Systems-level analysis of viruses representing three distinct taxonomic families—Coronaviridae (SARS-CoV-2), Filoviridae (Ebolavirus), and Orthomyxoviridae (Influenza virus)—revealed conserved host pathways and targets associated with diverse cellular functions, including endosomal trafficking, gap junction signaling, and cholesterol biosynthesis. The functional relevance of these predicted host targets was validated in cell-based infection assays using FDA-approved therapeutics to inhibit replication of human coronavirus 229E (HCoV-229E), vaccinia virus (VACV-WR), and Hantaan virus (HTNV), representing viruses with RNA and DNA genomes. Furthermore, quantitative global proteomic analysis of Seoul hantavirus infected human endothelial cells independently supported the relevance of AI-predicted host protein networks to viral replication. Collectively, these findings establish ViralTensors as an analytical framework for identifying conserved host dependencies across taxonomically diverse viruses and demonstrate the potential of targeting shared host cellular programs for the development of broad-spectrum antiviral therapeutics.

items.title: Use of Artificial Intelligence among Undergraduate Medical Students at Dhaka National Medical College: A Descriptive Cross-Sectional Study
items.abstract: Background: The use of artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly increasing among university students worldwide. However, little is known about how undergraduate medical students in Bangladesh engage with AI tools in their education. Objective: To assess the pattern of using AI and the self-reported knowledge and attitude regarding AI among undergraduate medical students of Dhaka National Medical College (DNMC). Methods: A descriptive cross-sectional study was conducted among 1st, 2nd, 3rd and 5th-year MBBS students of DNMC from December 2025 to July 2026 (4th-year students were excluded). By convenience type of non-probability sampling, 125 medical students completed a structured, self-administered questionnaire distributed as a Google Form through students' WhatsApp number. The questionnaire included sociodemographic data, patterns of AI use, and a 10-item, 5-point Likert scale for assessment of self-reported knowledge and attitudes (range 10 to 50). Data were analysed using descriptive statistics, the chi-square test, independent t-test, and ANOVA; p<0.05 was considered significant. Results: Mean age of 125 students was 21.7±1.7 years, among them 56.0% were female. Almost all respondents (97.6%) were familiar with AI. Most of them (89.6%) were current users, most commonly of ChatGPT (81.2%) and Gemini (32.1%). Majority of them (81.3%) thought that AI would be beneficial to their future career and 74.2% felt it should be taught to all medical students, 41.1% felt confident about replacement of medical specialities. Half of respondents (50.0%) were concerned about AI-generated misinformation, and 79.3% reported at least occasional difficulty verifying AI-generated academic content. The composite knowledge–attitude score (mean 37.2±6.0 of 50) rose significantly with academic year (p=0.023, driven by a 1st- versus 5th-year difference). Gender and current AI-use status were not significantly associated with the score. Conclusion: Most of the undergraduate medical students of DNMC have familiarity with use AIs and positive attitudes of it use for their learning. However, some of them are concerned about the misinformation may be produced by the AIs. Hence, structured AI-literacy training, from the first year of the MBBS curriculum, is a demand of the time. items.abstract: Background: Undergraduate healthcare students in India experience heavy academic pressure and exhausting hospital duties, yet rarely consult mental health professionals because of social stigma and fear of losing internal marks. Many students now turn to smartphone artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots late at night for private emotional comfort. This study assessed the prevalence of AI chatbot usage for emotional support, user perception, and emotional reliance among healthcare trainees in rural South India.

items.title: Using AI Chatbots to Support Reflective Practice in Transnational Teaching Practicums
items.abstract: This chapter examines the role of artificial intelligence (AI) as a reflective tool in language teacher education, with a particular focus on its potential to support professional learning during teaching practicums. Drawing on data from pre- and post-practicum group interviews, the study explores the experiences of 12 Vietnamese preservice Teaching English to Speakers of Other Languages (TESOL) teachers, who interacted with AI chatbots over an eight-week teaching practicum at a university in Thailand. The findings reveal that AI chatbots functioned as effective mediating tools, enabling participants to bridge TESOL theories and classroom-based practice. Additionally, the preservice teachers used AI chatbots to navigate cultural differences and to develop pedagogical approaches responsive to Thai classrooms. Most importantly, sustained engagement with AI chatbots throughout the practicum fostered reflective teaching practices among the participants. Based on these findings, the chapter discusses pedagogical implications for integrating AI chatbots to support reflective practice in TESOL teacher education.

items.title: Using artificial intelligence in insurance: ZhongAn Company as a case study
items.abstract: Subject. Application of artificial intelligence technologies in the operations of the Chinese internet insurance company ZhongAn – the first professional online insurer in China. Objectives. To conduct a comprehensive assessment of the impact of artificial intelligence technologies on the operational efficiency of the insurance company and to identify factors limiting the full realization of the potential of digital transformation. Methods. The study employed comparative analysis of operational indicators for 2019–2024, trend analysis of the dynamics of investments in research and development, financial analysis of performance indicators, SWOT analysis, and content analysis. Results. It has been established that the automation of the insurance company’s key business processes through artificial intelligence has reached extremely high levels: the underwriting automation rate is 99%, the reduction in claims settlement time is 87.5%, and employee productivity has increased 30‑fold. A paradox of efficiency has been identified: the growth in operational performance is accompanied by a persistently high level of consumer complaints, the opacity (non‑interpretability) of algorithms, risks of homogenization, and a shortage of personnel. A similar phenomenon has also been observed in the Russian insurance market. The hypothesis has been confirmed that technological efficiency alone is not a sufficient condition for sustainable profitability and consumer trust. Conclusions. For Russian insurers, ZhongAn’s experience demonstrates the need for the simultaneous development of technological infrastructure, human capital, and a customer‑oriented culture. The key success factor is the transformation from a technological pioneer into a responsible leader by ensuring the transparency of artificial intelligence systems and striking a balance between innovation and trust.

items.title: Using Cognitive Behavioural Approaches in Occupational Health Consultations
items.abstract: Fitness-to-work consultations in occupational health are often brief and framed by specific management referral questions. This can limit opportunities to explore beliefs, behaviours and wider psychological and social influences that sustain symptoms and contribute to ongoing work difficulties. This chapter argues that assessments are strengthened when grounded in a clear biopsychosocial framework and supported by the cognitive behavioural approach introduced earlier in the book. It demonstrates how concise biopsychosocial formulation helps practitioners understand how physical health, psychological processes, workplace demands and social factors interact. This enables the identification of modifiable maintaining mechanisms, such as unhelpful interpretations, avoidance patterns or reinforcing organisational practices, that influence functional capacity and return to work. A brief, work-focused method is presented using the ABC model and the 5 Ps formulation, which together form the practical backbone of the cognitive behavioural approach. A case example illustrates how focused enquiry and employee-centred assessment can reveal realistic levers for change and strengthen the clarity and defensibility of fitness-to-work reasoning.

items.title: Using Generative AI for Behavioural Research Effectively and Responsibly: a BR-UK Statement
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used across the behavioural research lifecycle. It may improve the efficiency and quality of research, but rapid, uncritical adoption carries risks to research integrity: algorithmic bias, ethical concerns around consent, privacy and plagiarism, erosion of researchers’ skills and public trust, and environmental costs. This Open Letter presents Behavioural Research UK’s (BR-UK) statement on using generative AI effectively and responsibly in behavioural research. It was informed by existing guidance and expert consultation. The statement sets out BR-UK’s four key propositions: (1) research ethics and integrity principles must include AI concerns; (2) AI should assist, but not replace, researchers through a human-in-the-loop approach; (3) rigorous evaluation of AI use is essential; and (4) coordinated stakeholder action is needed to move from identifying risks to practical solutions. It then provides recommendations and points to practical tools, such as decision aids and checklists for declaring AI use, for seven stakeholder groups, namely research-generating institutions, funders, publication outlets, behavioural research networks and communities, AI platform and tool providers, individual researchers, and research users. The statement will be reviewed annually until 2028, the duration of BR-UK, as technology and evidence evolve.

items.title: Using Tectonic Context to Help Constrain Rapid Earthquake Shaking Estimates
items.abstract: Abstract Accurate, readily available shaking estimates can improve situational awareness and rapid response efforts following a major earthquake. The spatial distribution of shaking relative to population and infrastructure has major implications for expected fatalities, damage, and disruptions. For large earthquakes, the location, size, and orientation of the causal fault plane (i.e., fault finiteness) play primary roles in determining the distribution of shaking. However, such a description of the causal fault is difficult to establish in the immediate aftermath of a major event, when observations are typically sparse and uncertain. However, during the time window between an event’s detection and the completion of quantitative constraints on the source, tectonic context can provide evidence for the rupture’s likely spatial orientation, thereby improving shaking estimates prior to formal finite-fault inversion results. Here, we propose a new method using tectonic context to describe a constrained, but still uncertain, source to improve early shaking estimates for large earthquakes. We demonstrate its implementation in the U.S. Geological Survey ShakeMap software by applying the proposed method to a catalog of 40 large (Mw>7), impactful global events from 2018 to 2026 and present an analysis of the results. We find that for 18 of the catalog events, the ShakeMap could be automatically constrained based on the seismotectonic context, whereas 14 events would require expert user input to determine whether a constrained approach is appropriate, and 8 events would not benefit from a constrained approach (but could be automatically identified). The results show that using seismotectonic context to constrain the source can substantially improve shaking estimates in the immediate minutes to hours following a major earthquake. We show a detailed comparison of the proposed (constrained) approach to the existing (unconstrained) approach for four earthquakes, each occurring in a distinct tectonic environment, to highlight the advantages and limitations of the method’s application.

items.title: Value Probes: Learned Value Functions for Beam-Search Red Teaming
items.abstract: Automated red-team auditing of language models is an important way to evaluate safety-relevant behaviors. These audits implicitly search a tree of possible conversation pathways: at each turn an auditor model decides which conversation to continue, and an LLM judge scores the dialogue. We emphasize that this auditing procedure is a Markov decision process, where states are the conversation history, actions are candidate responses, and rewards are judge scores for the target behavior. By adopting this perspective, we introduce two major improvements to auditing. First, we propose adopting beam search for the audit rather than relying on the auditor alone. We then interpret the problem of finding states that are likely to lead to problematic behavior as value estimation. Surprisingly, we show that this value function can be estimated by linear probing from the target model's activations to predict discounted future rewards - a method we term "Value Probes." By using Value Probes as a heuristic in our beam-search audit, we are able to substantially improve auditing success. Across 18 target behaviors and 3 scales of models, our approach raises peak audit scores by roughly 50% compared to (token-matched) standard auditing approaches. Furthermore, we show that Value Probes can be fit using off-policy data from smaller models. We also ablate individual components, and show that our method offers a comparably-performant and more efficient alternative to more expensive language model follow-ups. We hope these methods will improve language model auditing and lead to safer models.
